tekirdagrak-sb: Tekirdağ is a port town on the Sea of Marmara in Turkish Thrace, and its name has long been attached to rakı, the aniseed-flavoured grape spirit that Turkey drinks with meze and fish. Tekirdağ Rakısı was for decades a label of Tekel, the state spirits monopoly, and its character is often credited to the artesian water of nearby Çorlu. When Tekel's spirits business was privatised the brand passed to Mey İçki, now part of Diageo, and like all rakı it turns milky white when water is added.
araktouma-sb: Arak Touma is a Lebanese arak, grape spirit distilled again with green aniseed in the Levantine manner, and its makers have not published how the label began.
arakmassaya-sb: Massaya was founded in 1998 by the brothers Sami and Ramzi Ghosn at Tanaïl, in Lebanon's Bekaa Valley, on a family estate they had been forced to abandon during the civil war. They had returned in the early 1990s and brought in partners from two French wine families, the Bruniers of Vieux Télégraphe in Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Dominique Hébrard, formerly of Cheval Blanc. Arak was part of the plan from the start: the house distils it three times in copper alembics heated with vine wood, rests it in clay jars from the potters of Beit Chabab, and bottles it in distinctive blue glass.
anisdelmono-sb: The brothers Josep and Vicenç Bosch began making Anís del Mono in Badalona, just north of Barcelona, in 1870. Why the label shows a monkey is disputed: one story credits a pet at the factory, another reads it as a jab at the Darwin controversy, and the monkey is often said to wear the naturalist's face. In 1897 the firm ran one of Spain's first poster competitions, won by the painter Ramon Casas. The faceted bottle, registered in 1902, is still scraped with a spoon or stick as a percussion instrument in Spanish Christmas carols.
chinchondulce-sb: Chinchón Dulce is the sweet style of the aniseed spirit of Chinchón, the hill town south-east of Madrid whose name is a protected designation for anís, and the history of this particular label has not been published.
zibibsudanese-sb: Zibib, named from zabib, the Arabic word for raisin, is the name used in Egypt for the local aniseed spirit of the arak family, and no documented history has been found for a Sudanese bottling of it.
mastikapeshtera-sb: Peshtera Mastika is the aniseed spirit of Vinprom Peshtera, a distiller in the town of Peshtera at the foot of Bulgaria's Rhodope Mountains, and the company has not published a detailed account of how it began.
aalborgtaffelakvavit-sb: Aalborg Taffel Akvavit goes back to 1846, when Isidor Henius, a young immigrant distiller, set up in the Danish city of Aalborg and began producing a cleaner, more refined spirit than the local farm brandy. Flavoured with caraway, it was meant for the dinner table, which is what taffel means, and its red label became a familiar sight at Danish lunches. Henius's business became part of De Danske Spritfabrikker, formed in 1881, which made Aalborg the name most associated with Danish akvavit. The brand is now produced in Norway.
opanderson-sb: O.P. Anderson was introduced in 1891 at the Gothenburg Exhibition by the city firm O.P. Anderson & Son, at first under the name Gammal Fin 1ma Aquavit before it took the company's name. It is seasoned with caraway, anise and fennel and rested in oak barrels for about eight months, which gives it a pale straw colour. Usually described as the oldest Swedish akvavit brand still on sale, it is now produced by the Nordic drinks group Anora.
moutai-sb: Moutai takes its name from Maotai, a town on the Chishui River in Guizhou, where three private distilleries, Chengyi, Ronghe and Hengxing, were making sauce-aroma liquor from local sorghum before the People's Republic was founded. By the company's account the spirit won a medal at the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco, and in 1951 the three distilleries were merged into the state-owned Kweichow Moutai. Served at state banquets for decades, including the dinner for Richard Nixon's visit to China, it became the country's most famous baijiu.
wuliangye-sb: Wuliangye, from Yibin in Sichuan, traces its recipe to the Chen family, who are said to have refined a mixed-grain spirit there during the Ming dynasty, and the distillery still works fermentation pits it dates to that era. The spirit received its present name in 1909, when the local scholar Yang Huiquan proposed Wuliangye, meaning five-grain liquor, at a Yibin banquet, for its blend of sorghum, rice, glutinous rice, wheat and corn. In 1950 eight Yibin distilleries were merged into one state enterprise, which took the Wuliangye name in 1959.
luzhoulaojiao-sb: Luzhou Laojiao, in the Sichuan river city of Luzhou, dates its oldest fermentation pits to 1573, in the Ming dynasty, and has kept them in use ever since; its premium label, Guojiao 1573, is named for that year. The mud-lined pits are central to the strong-aroma style, which was first called Lu aroma after this distillery before it became the most widely made kind of baijiu in China. The modern company was formed in 1950, and its brewing techniques were included in China's first national list of intangible cultural heritage.
fenjiu-sb: Fenjiu comes from Xinghua, or Apricot Blossom, village in Fenyang, Shanxi, and takes its name from the nearby Fen River. Liquor-making in the area is very old, and tradition ties the village to a Tang-dynasty poem by Du Mu in which a herd boy points a traveller towards Apricot Blossom village to find a wine shop. Fenjiu is the model of the light-aroma style, fermented in earthenware jars buried in the ground rather than in mud pits, which gives a cleaner, more delicate spirit, and Beijing erguotou and Taiwanese kaoliang belong to the same family.
erguotouredstar-sb: Beijing's Red Star distillery was formed in 1949, when a dozen distilleries around the city were merged into one state enterprise, by the company's account in part to supply the celebrations for the founding of the People's Republic. Its spirit is erguotou, Beijing's own light-aroma baijiu. The name means second pot head: by the usual account, three brothers at the Yuanshenghao distillery in the 1680s found that their finest spirit ran while the second pot of cooling water sat atop the still. Red Star erguotou went on to become one of the most familiar spirits in northern China.
kinmenkaoliang-sb: Kinmen Kaoliang began in 1952 on Kinmen, the island group off the Fujian coast held by Taiwan, when the garrison commander Hu Lien set up an army-run distillery there, with the local distiller Yeh Hua-cheng overseeing its technical side. It took the name Jiulong River Distillery once a new plant was finished, and from 1956 became the Kinmen Distillery. Kaoliang is the Chinese word for sorghum, and the spirit is a light-aroma baijiu. Now owned by the Kinmen County government, the company remains an important source of revenue for the islands.
xifeng-sb: Xifeng comes from Fengxiang County, near Baoji in Shaanxi, an old seat of government in the Wei River valley with a long tradition of liquor-making. The name joins xi, west, with the first syllable of Fengxiang. Xifeng is the model of feng aroma, a baijiu style of its own: it is fermented in mud pits like strong-aroma spirits but aged in jiuhai, large containers woven from rattan and sealed on the inside, which gives it a fruity, earthy character between the strong and light styles.
jinmailangsesame-sb: Jinmailang Sesame is a sesame-aroma baijiu, a style first developed at the Jingzhi distillery in Shandong in the mid-twentieth century and named for a toasted note that comes from the process rather than from sesame, and no history of this particular label has been published.
iichiko-sb: Iichiko was launched in 1979 by Sanwa Shurui, a company founded in 1958 in Usa, in Ōita Prefecture on the island of Kyushu, which had turned from sake to shochu as competition from the big sake brewers grew. It is a mugi, or barley, shochu, light and clean in style, and its name is a local dialect phrase meaning roughly that's good. The name and the nickname shitamachi no Napoleon, the downtown Napoleon, were chosen through a public call in a local newspaper, and the brand's monthly posters, put up without a break since the 1980s, became well known across Japan.
kurokirishima-sb: Kirishima Shuzo was founded in 1916 by Kichisuke Enatsu in Miyakonojō, in Miyazaki Prefecture, near the Kirishima volcanic range on the border with Kagoshima. The company built its name on imo, or sweet potato, shochu, and in the late 1990s launched Kurokirishima, made with black kōji, the mould long used for Okinawan awamori. Kuro means black, and the brand did much to make black-kōji shochu a mainstream style across Japan.
satsumashiranami-sb: Satsuma Shuzo was founded in 1936 in Makurazaki, a fishing port at the southern tip of Kagoshima, in the old province of Satsuma, the heartland of sweet potato shochu. Its flagship, Satsuma Shiranami, takes a name meaning white waves. In the late 1970s the company's advertising promoted the local custom of cutting shochu six parts to four with hot water, and the campaign is credited with helping to spark Japan's shochu boom of the following decade, when shochu from the south reached drinkers across the country.
takarajun-sb: Takara Shuzo released Jun in 1977. The Kyoto company traces its roots to a sake brewery in Fushimi founded in 1842 and was incorporated under the Takara name in 1925. Jun is a kōrui shochu, made by continuous distillation into a clean, light spirit rather than in a pot still, the type that became the usual base for chūhai, the shochu highballs that spread through Japanese bars in the early 1980s. Jun has remained one of Takara's flagship labels since its launch.
lentokokuto-sb: Lento is made by Amami Ōshima Kaiun Shuzo in Uken, on the southern Japanese island of Amami Ōshima, a distillery founded in 1954 as Toda Shuzo. It is a kokutō shochu, distilled from brown sugar and rice kōji, a style that only the Amami Islands are permitted to make, under an arrangement that followed their return to Japanese rule after the Second World War. Lento is rested in tanks exposed to classical music, a process the distillery calls acoustic ageing, and its name is the musical term for slowly.
zuisenawamori-sb: Zuisen was founded in 1887 in Shuri, the old royal capital of Okinawa, and takes its name from a spring near the Zuisen Gate of Shuri Castle. Awamori is Okinawa's rice spirit, made from long-grain Thai rice and black kōji, and kusu is the term for awamori aged at least three years. The Battle of Okinawa destroyed much of the island's awamori heritage, including its old kōji strains, but a strain collected from Zuisen before the war was later found preserved at the University of Tokyo, and in 1999 the distillery released an awamori made with it.
jinrochamisul-sb: Jinro was founded in 1924 by Jang Hak-yeop in Yonggang, in what is now North Korea, and was re-established in the South after the Korean War. Chamisul, launched in 1998, was filtered through bamboo charcoal and presented as softer and cleaner than older soju; its name means real dew. Like most mass-market soju it is a diluted style, blended from neutral spirit and water, a method that spread after rice was restricted for distilling in the 1960s. A toad is the brand's emblem, and industry rankings have long listed Jinro as the largest-selling spirit brand in the world by volume.
chumchurum-sb: Chum Churum was launched in 2006 by Doosan, which promoted it as the first soju made with alkaline water, and passed to Lotte when Lotte acquired Doosan's liquor business in 2009; it is now made by Lotte Chilsung. The name means like the first time, and the brush lettering on the label came from the scholar and calligrapher Shin Young-bok, whose book of essays shared the title. A diluted soju in the soft, clean style of the period, it became the main rival to Jinro's Chamisul in Korea.
kornberentzen-sb: Johann Bernhard Tobias Berentzen founded his grain distillery in 1758 in Haselünne, a small town in the Emsland region of Lower Saxony, and the company is still based there. Korn is Germany's own grain spirit, distilled only from wheat, rye, barley, oats or buckwheat, and its name is protected. Berentzen registered its vom alten Fass grain brandy trademark in 1899, and in 1976 the brothers Friedrich and Hans Berentzen mixed wheat Korn with apple juice to create Apfelkorn, which made the family name familiar across Germany.
brannvinskane-sb: Brännvin, literally burnt wine, is the old Swedish word for distilled spirit, and this bottling named for Skåne, Sweden's southernmost province, has no published history of its own.
palmwineogogoro-sb: Ogogoro is the palm-wine spirit of southern Nigeria, long distilled in small village stills from the fermented sap of raffia and oil palms, and no documented history has been found for this particular bottling.
toddyarrack-sb: Ceylon arrack is Sri Lanka's spirit distilled from toddy, the naturally fermented sap of coconut palm flowers, and no documented history has been found for this particular bottling.
vichedelpacifico-sb: Viche is the cane spirit of the Afro-Colombian communities of Colombia's Pacific coast, distilled from fresh cane juice in small family stills and recently recognised in Colombian law as their ancestral heritage, and no history has been published for this particular bottling.
chirrinchiwayuu-sb: Chirrinchi is the home-distilled cane spirit of the Wayuu people of La Guajira, the desert peninsula Colombia shares with Venezuela, and no documented history has been found for this particular bottling.
ronligerohavana-sb: Ron ligero is the light, charcoal-filtered Cuban rum style that Facundo Bacardí Massó is usually credited with refining in Santiago de Cuba in the nineteenth century, and this Havana bottling has no published history of its own.
belizeanonebarrel-sb: One Barrel is a gold rum from Travellers Liquors of Belize City, one of the few rum distillers in Belize, and the company has not published how the blend began or how it got its name.
brown-derby: The usual account places the drink at the Vendôme Club, Billy Wilkerson's restaurant on Sunset Boulevard, around 1930. The same mix of whiskey, grapefruit and honey also circulated in print as the De Rigueur, but in Hollywood it took the name of the Brown Derby, the restaurant on Wilshire Boulevard built in the shape of a bowler hat. Both were fixtures of the film colony, and the drink has kept the restaurant's name long after the hat-shaped building closed.
blinker: The Blinker first appears in Patrick Gavin Duffy's Official Mixer's Manual of 1934, as rye whiskey shaken with grapefruit juice and grenadine. Nobody recorded why it was called the Blinker, and it slipped into obscurity until the cocktail historian Ted Haigh revived it in Vintage Spirits and Forgotten Cocktails, replacing the grenadine with raspberry syrup. Most modern bartenders follow his version, and the raspberry has effectively become the recipe.
camerons-kick: Cameron's Kick appears in Harry MacElhone's ABC of Mixing Cocktails in the early 1920s, from his years behind the bar in London before he took over Harry's New York Bar in Paris. Harry Craddock reprinted it in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930. It is unusual in pairing two whiskies, Scotch and Irish, with orgeat's almond richness bridging the smoky and the soft. Nobody has identified the Cameron of the title or explained the kick.
chancellor: The Chancellor, a stirred drink of Scotch, tawny port and dry vermouth in the family of the Rob Roy, has no firmly documented creator, bar or date, and nobody has explained which chancellor its name honours.
algonquin: The Algonquin takes its name from the Algonquin Hotel on West 44th Street in New York, home of the Round Table, the circle of writers and critics including Dorothy Parker and Robert Benchley who lunched there daily through the Prohibition years. No record ties the drink to the hotel's own bar or to the Round Table, and its creator is unknown. Its unusual pairing of rye with pineapple has nonetheless kept it in cocktail books for generations.
monte-carlo-cocktail: The Monte Carlo is usually traced to David Embury's The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks of 1948, where rye whiskey is sweetened with Bénédictine and seasoned with Angostura. Embury did not say who created it, and the name borrows the glamour of Monaco's casino town. Bénédictine, launched in Fécamp in Normandy by Alexandre Le Grand, has a recipe said to be known to only a handful of people at a time, and its herbal sweetness lets it stand in for vermouth.
preakness: The Preakness takes its name from the Preakness Stakes, the second race of America's Triple Crown, run at Pimlico in Baltimore. The race itself honours the colt Preakness, winner of the Dinner Party Stakes on the day Pimlico opened. Who first mixed the cocktail is not recorded, and it is a less familiar race-day drink than the Black-Eyed Susan, the race's official cocktail. The winner's garland of black-eyed Susans is traditionally made from other flowers painted to match, since the real ones do not bloom in time for the race in May.
palmetto: Harry Craddock printed the Palmetto in The Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 as St. Croix rum and Italian vermouth with orange bitters. It comes from an era when bartenders moved rum, whiskey and brandy freely through the same templates, before each spirit was given its own world. The name has never been explained, though the palmetto palm is the emblem of South Carolina. Modern bartenders usually make it with an aged rum.
pegu-club: The Pegu Club was a British club outside Rangoon, in colonial Burma, whose members were senior officials, officers and businessmen, and it took its name from the Pegu River. Its house cocktail first appeared in print in Harry MacElhone's ABC of Mixing Cocktails of 1923, and The Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 noted that it had travelled the world. The drink outlived both the club and the empire, and in 2005 the New York bartender Audrey Saunders gave its name to her influential bar on West Houston Street.
saratoga: The Saratoga appears in the 1887 edition of Jerry Thomas's Bar-Tender's Guide, published two years after his death, as a stirred drink splitting its base between brandy and rye. It is named for Saratoga Springs in upstate New York, the spa town whose mineral springs, racetrack and grand hotels made it one of America's leading summer resorts of the nineteenth century. The town also lent its name to the Saratoga chip and the Saratoga trunk.
journalist: The Journalist, a gin drink with both vermouths, orange liqueur, lemon and bitters, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator and no explanation of its name.
twentieth-century: The Twentieth Century was created by the British bartender C. A. Tuck and printed in William J. Tarling's Café Royal Cocktail Book of 1937. It was named for the 20th Century Limited, the New York Central Railroad's luxury express between New York and Chicago, whose passengers boarded along a red carpet, a custom often credited with giving English the phrase red carpet treatment. The train ran until 1967, and the drink was revived by modern bartenders exploring the Café Royal book.
corpse-reviver-no-1: Corpse revivers were a family of so-called restoratives served on both sides of the Atlantic from the nineteenth century, and the name was used for several unrelated drinks. Harry Craddock fixed two of them in The Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930: the all-brandy No. 1 and No. 2, the gin, Lillet, Cointreau and lemon drink that is better known today. Craddock gave No. 1 a tongue-in-cheek serving note but no creator, and it remains the brown-spirit sibling.
satans-whiskers: Satan's Whiskers appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 in two versions, straight with Grand Marnier and curled with orange curaçao, with no recorded creator and no reason given for its devilish name.
maidens-prayer: The Maiden's Prayer, a gin sour sharpened with orange liqueur and both lemon and orange juice, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 beside relatives such as the White Lady, with no recorded creator and no explanation of its name.
leap-year: Harry Craddock created the Leap Year for the Savoy Hotel's celebration of 29 February 1928, and printed it two years later in The Savoy Cocktail Book with the claim that it had prompted more proposals than any other cocktail. The joke rests on the old tradition that women could propose marriage on leap day. Craddock, an English bartender who had worked in American hotel bars until Prohibition sent him home, was then head bartender of the Savoy's American Bar.
lucien-gaudin: The Lucien Gaudin is usually placed in Paris in the late 1920s, and it honours the French fencer Lucien Gaudin, who won Olympic gold in both foil and épée at the Amsterdam Games of 1928. Its creator is not recorded. The drink lay forgotten for decades before modern bartenders took it up as a lighter, drier member of the Negroni's extended family.
millionaire: Several unrelated drinks have carried the name Millionaire, and this rye sour with orange curaçao, grenadine and egg white appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 beside a different Millionaire of Jamaica rum, sloe gin and apricot brandy, with no recorded creator for either.
ampersand: The Ampersand, an equal-parts mix of Old Tom gin, brandy and sweet vermouth finished with curaçao, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator and no reason given for naming a drink after a punctuation mark.
colonial: The Colonial is an American gin sour of grapefruit juice and maraschino, and its creator, first printing and the meaning of its name are not documented.
nuclear-daiquiri: Gregor de Gruyther created the Nuclear Daiquiri at LAB, the influential bar in London's Soho, around 2005. He kept the Daiquiri's lime-and-sugar logic but built it on Wray & Nephew overproof Jamaican rum with green Chartreuse and falernum. The name is usually put down to its luminous green colour and the intensity of its two main spirits. It spread through London's bartending community and then internationally, becoming one of the most widely known modern variations on the Daiquiri.
vieux-mot: Don Lee created the Vieux Mot at PDT in New York's East Village in 2007, the year St-Germain elderflower liqueur was launched. Lee was one of the original bartenders at PDT, the speakeasy entered through a phone booth inside a hot-dog shop. The name is French for old word, a nod to the Last Word, whose shape it echoes. As St-Germain appeared on back bars across America, the Vieux Mot was one of the drinks that showed bartenders what to do with it.
the-business: The Business, gin shaken with honey and lime, is a modern London relative of the Bee's Knees whose creator and date are not firmly documented, and its name is British slang for something first-rate.
weeski: The Weeski is a modern stirred drink of Irish whiskey, Lillet Blanc and orange liqueur, and who first made it, and where, is not firmly documented.
ford-cocktail: The Ford was in print by the mid-1890s, in George Kappeler's Modern American Drinks, compiled while he was head bartender at New York's Holland House, and Hugo Ensslin carried it into his Recipes for Mixed Drinks two decades later. It belongs to the late-Victorian family of Old Tom gin drinks seasoned with Bénédictine and bitters. Which Ford it honours has never been established, but the drink was in print before the carmaker's name was famous.
bywater: Chris Hannah created the Bywater at Arnaud's French 75 Bar in the French Quarter of New Orleans and named it for Bywater, the neighbourhood downriver of the Faubourg Marigny. Hannah, long the head bartender at French 75, was one of the leading figures of the city's modern cocktail revival.
elder-fashion: The Elder Fashion is credited to Phil Ward at Death & Co in New York in 2007, the year St-Germain elderflower liqueur reached American bars. Ward built it on gin in the Old Fashioned manner, letting the liqueur do the work of the sugar. Ward later opened Mayahuel, a New York bar devoted to agave spirits.
silver-monk: The Silver Monk is a modern tequila sour seasoned with Chartreuse, cucumber and mint, and accounts of who first made it, and in which city, do not agree.
vaina: The vaina is a Chilean egg drink of port or another sweet fortified wine shaken with egg yolk and sugar, often with brandy or pisco and a dusting of cinnamon or cocoa, made at home rather than credited to any bar or creator.
sucumbe: Sucumbé is a frothy Bolivian hot drink of milk whipped with egg, cinnamon and singani, the country's grape brandy, made at home for cold nights and Christmas, and no creator or date is recorded.
crema-de-vie: Crema de vie is a Cuban home-made holiday cream of rum, egg yolk and sweetened milk, a relative of eggnog and Puerto Rico's coquito, passed between families rather than bars and with no recorded creator or date.
guavaberry-colada: Guavaberries are small wild fruits of the hills of Sint Maarten and neighbouring islands, and islanders have long steeped them in rum with sugar and spice to make a folk liqueur that belongs to Christmas, when singers go from house to house with guavaberry songs. The Guavaberry Emporium in Philipsburg bottles the liqueur commercially, and the colada blends it with coconut cream and pineapple in the manner of the Piña Colada, though nobody is recorded as its creator.
clericot: Clericot is a fruit-and-wine punch served by the jug in Mexico, made with red or white wine, and the same drink appears as clericó in Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay. Its name is usually traced to the English claret cup, a nineteenth-century punch of claret, fruit and soda, which travelled through the Spanish-speaking world in adapted forms. Recipes change with the season and the household, and no single creator or date is recorded.
te-con-te: Té con té, black tea spiked with singani, Bolivia's grape brandy, is a hot drink of cold nights in La Paz and across the highlands, and no one is recorded as having first made it.
blue-moon-cocktail: The Blue Moon is an early twentieth-century gin drink coloured and scented with violet liqueur, its recipe varying from book to book, and its creator and first printing are not settled.
bronx-terrace: The Bronx Terrace, a drier, lime-sharpened variation on the Bronx without its sweet vermouth or orange juice, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, and who devised it and which terrace it names are not recorded.
clover-leaf: The Clover Leaf, a Clover Club finished with a mint leaf on the foam, appears alongside its parent in interwar books such as Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, and the Clover Club was named for a Philadelphia gentlemen's club of lawyers, writers and businessmen, but who first added the mint is not recorded.
dempsey: The Dempsey, an unusual pairing of gin and apple brandy, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator, and it is usually taken to honour Jack Dempsey, world heavyweight champion from 1919 to 1926.
knickerbocker: Jerry Thomas printed the Knickerbocker in his Bar-Tender's Guide of 1862 as the Knickerbocker à la Monsieur, alongside a lighter à la Madame, which makes it older than the Manhattan and the Martini. It was a summer drink, built over shaved ice. The name comes from Knickerbocker, the nickname for old New Yorkers, popularised by Washington Irving's comic history of the city, written under the pen name Diedrich Knickerbocker.
merry-widow: Several unrelated drinks carry the name Merry Widow, after Franz Lehár's operetta, the theatrical sensation of the years before the First World War, which also gave its name to a fashionable wide-brimmed hat. The aromatic gin version appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, and no creator is recorded for any of them. The name reflects a habit of the age, when bartenders often named drinks after the hit shows of the day.
old-etonian: The Old Etonian, a short gin-and-Lillet drink scented with crème de noyaux, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator, and its name refers to the former pupils of Eton College.
opera: The Opera, a stirred gin drink built around Dubonnet and maraschino, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator, and the book does not say which opera, if any, it honours.
orange-blossom: The Orange Blossom became one of the signature drinks of American Prohibition, when the gin of the speakeasies often needed disguising and orange juice did the job. Harry Craddock included it in The Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, and other books of the period give versions with vermouth or grenadine. Its creator is unknown, and it is said to have faded from favour once good gin was legal again.
poets-dream: The Poet's Dream, gin and dry vermouth sweetened with Bénédictine, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator and no poet named.
red-snapper: By the usual account, when Fernand Petiot moved from Harry's New York Bar in Paris to the King Cole Bar at New York's St. Regis Hotel in 1934, he brought with him the tomato-juice drink he said he had first mixed in Paris. Vodka was still scarce in America, so he made it with gin, and the story goes that the hotel thought the name Bloody Mary too coarse for its bar, so it was listed as the Red Snapper. The gin version kept that name, while the vodka Bloody Mary became the brunch standard.
royal-bermuda-yacht-club: Trader Vic printed the Royal Bermuda Yacht Club cocktail in his Bartender's Guide of 1947, a Daiquiri-style rum sour named for the yacht club in Hamilton. The club itself was founded in 1844 and received its royal patronage from Prince Albert the following year, and its clubhouse stands on the Hamilton waterfront. Who first mixed the drink, and whether it was ever a house drink at the club, is not recorded.
seventh-heaven: The Seventh Heaven appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, which prints more than one drink under the name, and the cherry-scented grapefruit sour that survives has no recorded creator, its name the old idiom for perfect happiness.
tipperary: The Tipperary appears in Hugo Ensslin's Recipes for Mixed Drinks of 1916, and Harry Craddock carried it into The Savoy Cocktail Book. Its name presumably comes from the song rather than the county: 'It's a Long Way to Tipperary', written in 1912, became the marching song of British soldiers in the First World War. Modern bartenders often cut back the Chartreuse and vermouth to tame the drink's sweetness and let the Irish whiskey show.
waldorf: The Waldorf takes its name from the original Waldorf-Astoria on Fifth Avenue, whose long bar produced or popularised a remarkable share of pre-Prohibition drinks, including the Rob Roy and the Bronx. Hugo Ensslin printed a Waldorf of whiskey, Italian vermouth, absinthe and bitters, and the hotel's recipes were later gathered by Albert Stevens Crockett in Old Waldorf Bar Days. The building itself was demolished to make way for the Empire State Building.
yale: The Yale is one of several pre-Prohibition cocktails named for American universities, a gin drink tinted blue with violet liqueur, presumably for Yale blue, and no creator is recorded.
fallen-angel: The Fallen Angel, a gin sour seasoned with white crème de menthe and Angostura, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator and no explanation of its name.
napoleon: The Napoleon, almost neat gin seasoned with dashes of curaçao, Dubonnet and Fernet-Branca, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator, its name presumably borrowing the French emperor's prestige.
wassail: Wassail goes back to Anglo-Saxon England, where wes hál, be well, was a toast answered with drinc hál, and the same greeting has Old Norse relatives. By the Middle Ages the word named both the toast and the spiced ale, often with roasted apples, that was shared from a communal bowl at midwinter while singers went door to door. In the cider counties of the West of England the custom survives as orchard wassailing in January, when villagers toast the apple trees and sing to them for a good harvest.
smoking-bishop: Bishop was an eighteenth-century English punch of port, or sometimes claret, mulled with oranges or lemons roasted until charred and stuck with cloves, then sweetened and spiced. It had relatives named for other ranks of the church, from Archbishop to Pope, depending on the wine used, and the smoking presumably refers to the steaming bowl. The drink owes its lasting fame to Charles Dickens, who has a reformed Scrooge promise Bob Cratchit a bowl of Smoking Bishop at the end of A Christmas Carol.
lambs-wool: Lamb's wool is an old English drink of hot ale, sugar and spice poured over roasted apples until their burst flesh rises as a pale froth, which is usually said to have given it its name. It belonged to Twelfth Night and other winter feast days, often served from the wassail bowl, and it turns up in seventeenth-century writing, including Robert Herrick's poem on the Twelfth Night revels. Recipes vary in their spices, but the roasted apple and its woolly froth are constant.
syllabub: Syllabub was a favourite of Tudor and Stuart England: sweet wine, cider or sack mixed with cream or milk and sugar, sometimes lemon, until it frothed. The earliest versions were said to be made by milking a cow straight into a bowl of spiced wine or cider so the warm milk foamed as it fell, a technique that kept syllabub a country dish. Later cooks whipped the cream until it held its shape, and by the eighteenth century it was served in glasses as a dessert, eaten with a spoon.
negus: Negus is named after Colonel Francis Negus, an English courtier and politician of the early eighteenth century. The story goes that during a heated argument over wine, he proposed diluting it with hot water, sugar, lemon and nutmeg, and the mixture took his name. Made with port by the Victorian era, negus was a standard offering at balls and evening parties, and it appears in Jane Austen's Mansfield Park and in several novels by Charles Dickens.
posset: The posset was a staple of English kitchens from the late Middle Ages into the eighteenth century, made by curdling hot milk with ale, wine or sack. It was served in special posset pots with a spout near the base, so the drinker could sip the warm liquid from below while eating the soft curd on top with a spoon. Shakespeare's Lady Macbeth drugs the possets of Duncan's guards, and the modern lemon posset dessert keeps the name without the alcohol.
brandy-sour: The Cyprus brandy sour is usually traced to the Forest Park Hotel in Platres, a hill resort in the Troodos mountains above Limassol, in the 1930s, after the Haggipavlu family had introduced the first blended brandy made on the island. The often-told story is that a barman named Sourmelis made it for the young King Farouk of Egypt so that it would pass for iced tea, though Farouk is reported not to have drunk alcohol at all. Whatever its start, the drink spread from the mountains to the coastal resorts and the capital.
kinnie-and-gin: Kinnie, the bitter-orange and wormwood soft drink that the Maltese brewer Simonds Farsons Cisk launched in 1952, is a familiar Maltese partner for gin, though nobody is recorded as having first mixed the two.
rum-and-raspberry: Rum and raspberry, white rum lengthened with raspberry cordial and soda, is a simple long drink associated with southern Africa that has no recorded creator or date.
fort-point: The Fort Point is a modern Manhattan relative made bittersweet with Punt e Mes, Bénédictine and maraschino, and its creator is not firmly documented; the name is shared with a different rye drink created in San Francisco, home of the old fort beneath the Golden Gate Bridge.
kentucky-maid: Sam Ross created the Kentucky Maid at Milk & Honey in New York in the mid-2000s as a bourbon answer to the Southside, the gin, lime and mint drink associated with Prohibition-era speakeasies. He added muddled cucumber, which the mint ties to the bourbon. Ross, who came to New York from Melbourne, also created the Penicillin and the Paper Plane, and the Kentucky Maid has travelled widely as one of the signature drinks of the Milk & Honey school.
death-flip: Chris Hysted-Adams created the Death Flip at the Black Pearl in Melbourne around 2010, pairing tequila with two strongly herbal liqueurs and binding them with a whole egg. On paper it read like a dare, but it won over the city's bartenders and travelled from there to cocktail bars around the world, becoming one of the most widely known Australian contributions to the modern canon. The name plays on the flip, the old family of drinks shaken or stirred with egg.
gordons-breakfast: Gordon's Breakfast is a modern savoury gin sour of muddled cucumber and lime seasoned with Worcestershire and hot sauce, and neither its creator nor the Gordon of its name is firmly documented.
bermuda-rose: The Bermuda Rose is a pink interwar gin sour of apricot brandy, grenadine and lemon whose creator and first printing are not firmly recorded.
blackthorn: The Blackthorn of Irish whiskey, dry vermouth and absinthe appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, while an unrelated sloe-gin drink of the same name circulated in the same era, and no creator is recorded for either.
charlie-chaplin: The Charlie Chaplin was a house drink of the original Waldorf-Astoria in New York, named while Chaplin's silent comedies of the mid-1910s made him one of the most recognisable people in the world. The hotel's pre-Prohibition recipes, this one included, were later gathered by Albert Stevens Crockett in Old Waldorf Bar Days. Its creator at the Waldorf bar is not recorded, and the equal-parts recipe has survived largely unchanged.
claridge: The Claridge, a Martini softened with apricot brandy and orange liqueur, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, which does not say who created it or whether it honours Claridge's in London or the Hôtel Claridge in Paris.
cornell: The Cornell, a simple foamy gin sour with maraschino and egg white, is one of the early twentieth-century cocktails named for American universities, and no creator is recorded.
deep-sea: The Deep Sea, a dry Martini perfumed with a dash of absinthe and orange bitters, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator and no explanation of its name.
delmonico: The Delmonico, a stirred drink of gin, brandy and both vermouths, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator, and it presumably takes its name from Delmonico's, the New York restaurant that set the standard for American fine dining in the nineteenth century.
dubonnet-cocktail: Gin and Dubonnet was in print by 1930, when Harry Craddock listed the pairing in The Savoy Cocktail Book, where it also appears as the Zaza. Dubonnet itself was created in Paris in 1846 by the wine merchant Joseph Dubonnet as a quinine-flavoured aperitif wine. The mix took on a royal association: Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother was well known for her gin and Dubonnet, and it was widely reported to be a pre-lunch choice of her daughter, Queen Elizabeth II.
emerald: The Emerald is a Manhattan made with Irish whiskey and named for the Emerald Isle, and it has no documented creator or date.
fine-and-dandy: The Fine and Dandy, one of the many interwar gin sours made with orange liqueur, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator, and its name is an idiom of the period for everything being in order.
flying-dutchman: The Flying Dutchman, little more than gin with a dash of orange liqueur, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator, and takes its name from the legendary ghost ship doomed to sail forever.
golden-dawn: The Golden Dawn is credited to Tom Buttery of the Berkeley Hotel in London, whose recipe won the International Cocktail Competition in 1930, and The Savoy Cocktail Book recorded it the same year. A dash of grenadine sinking through the glass gives the sunrise of its name, four decades before the Tequila Sunrise made the effect famous. Later recipes vary, and some drop the grenadine altogether.
green-dragon: The Green Dragon, an unusual meeting of gin, kümmel, crème de menthe and lemon, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator, and its name was also a common one for English inns.
hula-hula: The Hula-Hula, a simple mix of gin, orange juice and curaçao, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator, its Hawaiian name arriving a few years before the first American tiki bars.
jockey-club: The Jockey Club, an almond-scented gin sour with crème de noyaux, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, which does not say who created it or which of the racing clubs of that name it honours.
judge-jr: The Judge Jr. seems to take its name from Judge Jr., the pen name under which the American humour magazine Judge published Here's How, a cocktail booklet, in 1927, when printing drink recipes during Prohibition was legally dubious. The drink, a gin-and-rum sour coloured with grenadine, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, and no individual creator is recorded. Judge was a long-running rival of the humour magazine Puck.
leave-it-to-me: Leave It To Me appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 in two different versions, one with apricot brandy, lemon and grenadine and one with raspberry syrup and maraschino, and neither has a recorded creator.
lone-tree: The Lone Tree, a Martini split between French and Italian vermouth, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator, and the lone tree of its title has never been identified.
moulin-rouge: The Moulin Rouge is one of several unrelated drinks named for the Paris cabaret beneath the red windmill on the Boulevard de Clichy, and this sloe-gin version from the interwar bar books has no recorded creator.
obituary: The Obituary is the house drink of Lafitte's Blacksmith Shop on Bourbon Street in New Orleans, a French colonial building that claims to be among the oldest structures used as a bar in the United States and is still lit largely by candles. By local legend the privateer Jean Lafitte used the blacksmith's shop as a front for smuggling. Who first mixed the Obituary, and why it carries such a mournful name, are not recorded.
palm-beach: The Palm Beach is an interwar gin and grapefruit drink named for the Florida resort, printed in several forms in the books of the period, and its creator is unknown.
pall-mall: The Pall Mall, a Perfect Martini scented with white crème de menthe, takes its name from the London street at the heart of gentlemen's clubland, itself named for pall-mall, a mallet-and-ball game played there in the seventeenth century, and no creator is recorded.
park-avenue: The Park Avenue is an interwar gin drink of sweet vermouth and pineapple juice named for New York's grand residential avenue, and no creator is recorded.
perfect-lady: The Perfect Lady is credited to Sidney Cox of the Grosvenor House Hotel on Park Lane in London, whose recipe won the British Empire Cocktail Competition in 1936. It belongs to the White Lady family of gin sours, with peach brandy in place of the orange liqueur.
princes-smile: The Prince's Smile, an apple-and-apricot gin sour, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator, and which prince is smiling is not recorded either.
princeton: The Princeton, Old Tom gin with orange bitters finished with port poured gently so that it settles beneath the gin, is one of the cocktails named for American universities around the turn of the twentieth century, and no creator is recorded.
racquet-club: The Racquet Club is a club Martini of gin and dry vermouth with orange bitters that shares its name with New York's Racquet and Tennis Club, and it has no recorded creator.
rolls-royce: The Rolls-Royce, a Perfect Martini given a herbal edge with Bénédictine, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator, its name borrowing the prestige of the British carmaker.
royal-smile: The Royal Smile, a pink sour of gin, calvados, grenadine and lemon, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator.
silver-bullet: The Silver Bullet, a short gin drink sharpened with lemon and scented with the caraway of kümmel, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator, and its name borrows the folklore weapon against werewolves.
straits-sling: The Straits Sling takes its name from the Straits Settlements, the British colony that included Singapore, and it is generally treated as the drier ancestor of the Singapore Sling. Robert Vermeire printed it in 1922 in Cocktails: How to Mix Them, presenting it as a Singapore drink. The Raffles Hotel credits its own Singapore Sling to the bartender Ngiam Tong Boon around 1915, but the drink it serves today is far sweeter and heavy with pineapple.
sunshine-cocktail: Several unrelated drinks were called the Sunshine in the bar books of the interwar years, and this short gin-and-vermouth version tinted with grenadine has no recorded creator.
tango-cocktail: The Tango appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator, and it takes its name from the Argentine dance whose craze reached London and Paris on the eve of the First World War.
ulanda: The Ulanda, gin and orange liqueur perfumed with a dash of absinthe, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator, and nobody has established what or whom its name refers to.
union-jack: The Union Jack, gin and sloe gin with a dash of grenadine, is an interwar drink whose creator is not recorded and whose name presumably plays on the colours of the flag.
wembley: The Wembley, gin and dry vermouth with apricot brandy and calvados, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator, and its name presumably recalls the British Empire Exhibition held at Wembley in north-west London in 1924 and 1925.
white-rose: The White Rose, a pale gin sour of maraschino, orange and lemon with egg white, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator.
whizz-bang: The Whizz Bang, one of the few Scotch drinks in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, has no recorded creator, and its name is First World War soldiers' slang for a German field shell.
yellow-daisy: The Yellow Daisy, an orange-scented gin drink, appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 with no recorded creator, and its name borrows the daisy, one of the oldest families of mixed drinks.
zaza: The Zaza appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, the same gin-and-Dubonnet pairing the book also calls the Dubonnet Cocktail. It is named for Zaza, a play by Pierre Berton and Charles Simon about a music-hall singer, first staged in Paris in 1898, which became an international hit and was filmed several times in Hollywood. No creator is recorded, and the drink has outlived the play.
kon-tiki: The Kon-Tiki is an aged-rum tiki drink named for Thor Heyerdahl's balsa raft, whose Pacific crossing put the name on restaurants, motels and drinks, and who first mixed it, and when, is not documented.
mariners-grog: The Mariner's Grog is a Hollywood tiki recipe in the Don the Beachcomber manner whose creator and date are not well documented, and its name borrows the Royal Navy's grog, the rum ration that Admiral Edward Vernon ordered to be diluted with water.
outrigger: The Outrigger is a tiki rum drink named for the side float that steadied Polynesian canoes on their long ocean crossings, but several unrelated drinks have used the name and who first mixed this one is not documented.
pi-yi: The Pi Yi is a pineapple-served drink from the menus of Don the Beachcomber, the Hollywood bar opened by Ernest Raymond Beaumont Gantt, later known as Donn Beach, which is credited with launching the tiki bar. Serving drinks in hollowed fruit became a tiki convention, and the Pi Yi's exact date and the meaning of its name are not recorded.
port-au-prince: The Port au Prince is a Don the Beachcomber recipe from Hollywood, built on Haitian rum and named for the capital of the country that made it. Haitian rhum is often distilled from fresh cane juice rather than molasses, which gives it a grassy, vegetal character quite unlike the Jamaican and Demerara rums that dominate most tiki recipes. Its exact date is not recorded, and the recipe reached modern bars through tiki historians' work on the Beachcomber files.
tortuga: The Tortuga is a Trader Vic recipe from Oakland, and Trader Vic's books and menus give more than one version of it. It is named for Tortuga, the island off the north coast of Haiti that served as a base for buccaneers in the seventeenth century, the real pirate haven behind much of the tiki aesthetic. The drink's exact date is not recorded.
tropical-itch: Harry Yee created the Tropical Itch at the Hawaiian Village Hotel in Waikiki in 1957, as Hawaii's tourist boom gathered pace. Yee, who also devised the Blue Hawaii, gave it a bamboo backscratcher as a souvenir garnish, a joke on the drink's name, and the prop became its signature. He is remembered as one of the key figures of Hawaiian tiki, and versions of the drink still appear on Honolulu menus.
coconut-grog: The Coconut Grog is a spiced rum drink with coconut cream in the Don the Beachcomber manner, a long way from the watered naval rum that gave grog its name, and its creator and date are not firmly documented.
demerara-dry-float: The Demerara Dry Float comes from Don the Beachcomber's Hollywood bar and reached modern bars through the tiki historian Jeff Berry's work on surviving Beachcomber recipes. Its defining feature is the overproof Demerara rum floated on top, which perfumes the first sips. Demerara, the Guyanese river and colony whose sugar estates gave the rum style its name, is still the name for rum from Guyana.
japanese-cocktail: Jerry Thomas printed the Japanese Cocktail in his Bar-Tender's Guide of 1862. By the usual account he named it for the first Japanese diplomatic mission to the United States, which drew huge, curious crowds when it visited New York in 1860 and is said to have stayed near Thomas's bar on Broadway. Its almond sweetness comes from orgeat, and it is one of the oldest named cocktails still made close to its original recipe.
brandy-smash: The smash was a fashionable American drink of the 1840s and 1850s, and Jerry Thomas fixed it in print in his Bar-Tender's Guide of 1862, treating it as a smaller relation of the julep. Brandy was the usual base. The name presumably describes the pounding of the mint. The smash later fell from fashion, but bartenders revived the family in the 2000s, when the Whiskey Smash, usually credited to Dale DeGroff and made with lemon, became a modern standard.
gin-sling: In the eighteenth century a sling was a mix of spirit, water and sugar, often grated with nutmeg, served hot or cold on both sides of the Atlantic, and gin was a natural base in London. When an early American newspaper first defined the cocktail in print, it described it as a bittered sling, a sling with bitters added. The origin of the word sling is uncertain, and no single creator is recorded. Later slings gained lemon and soda, leading eventually to the Singapore Sling.
